title: Hebrew and Aramaic compared

objectives.can: Set an Aramaic passage beside Hebrew: cognate vocabulary, false friends, and the constructions each language uses for the same job.

explanation.summary: A reader who knows Hebrew can use it to see the family likeness in Aramaic, and can also be led astray by it. This lesson sets real Aramaic words beside Hebrew words, separates true cognates from words whose senses have shifted, and gathers the constructions in which the two languages do the same job differently.

sections.heading: Cognates seen across the vocabulary
body: Lesson A0.1.3 taught the regular consonant correspondences. They now apply to the vocabulary of the whole course. The Aramaic verb for 'return' begins with a tav where the Hebrew verb for returning has a shin. The Aramaic verb for 'sacrifice' and the Aramaic noun for a record or memorandum begin with a dalet, where the Hebrew verb and the Hebrew noun for 'remembrance' have a zayin. These are the correspondences ד with ז and ת with שׁ.

Vowels differ as well. The Aramaic word for 'generation' has an ā vowel where the Hebrew word has ō. The Aramaic words for 'heart' and 'head' have different vowels from the Hebrew words, and the Aramaic noun for 'kingdom' is listed without the final ת that the Hebrew noun has, although Aramaic forms with endings keep it, as in the word for 'my kingdom' in Daniel 4:33.
In every pair, the two words are cognates and not the same word. Each one is learned in its own language: the table gives the pairs, and the Aramaic form is the one to know.

sections.heading: False friends: same letters, other senses
body: Some Aramaic words have the same letters as a Hebrew word and a different sense. The commonest Aramaic verb for 'make' or 'do' is עֲבַד, as in Daniel 4:32, where God 'does' as He wills. The Hebrew verb עָבַד means 'work' or 'serve', and Hebrew uses עָשָׂה for 'make' and 'do'. The Aramaic verb for 'find', שְׁכַח, looks like the Hebrew verb שָׁכַח, which means 'forget'; Hebrew uses מָצָא for 'find'. A reader who guesses from Hebrew would read Daniel 2:25, 'I have found a man', as a statement about forgetting.

A smaller shift is one of frequency and range. The Aramaic noun מִלָּה is the ordinary word for 'word' and also for 'matter' or 'thing', as in Daniel 2:5, 'the matter is certain with me'. The Hebrew noun מִלָּה means 'word' or 'speech' and occurs far less often than דָּבָר, which is the usual Hebrew word for 'word' and 'thing'. The Aramaic verb אֲמַר means 'say' and, in Daniel 3:13, 'command'; the Hebrew verb אָמַר means 'say'. And the Aramaic verb בְּעָא means 'ask' or 'seek', as in Daniel 6:8, where the Hebrew verb בָּעָה is rare and means 'inquire' and 'swell'; Hebrew uses בָּקַשׁ for 'seek'.
The rule is the one given in A0.1.3: learn each Aramaic word from its Aramaic uses, and bring the Hebrew in afterwards as a comparison.

sections.heading: The same job, done differently
body: The two languages differ in several constructions that every reader of Daniel and Ezra meets. The first is the word 'the'. Hebrew puts a prefix ה- on the noun. Aramaic ends the noun in the determined state, -ָא, as in the Aramaic for 'the king' and 'the heavens'. The second is the relative. Aramaic uses דִּי, which also serves as 'of', 'that' and 'because'; Hebrew uses אֲשֶׁר.

Third, 'there is' is אִיתַי in Aramaic, as in Daniel 2:10, and יֵשׁ in Hebrew; 'there is not' is אֵין in Hebrew. Fourth, a wish or command in the third person of the verb 'be' is formed in Aramaic with a prefix לְ-, as in Daniel 2:20, where the name of God is to be blessed. Hebrew uses a jussive with the prefix י-.

Fifth, the narrative. The Hebrew of the narrative books runs on a chain of verbs in the wayyiqtol form: the Hebrew texts of the library hold over fourteen thousand. The verbs of the Aramaic texts are tagged only as perfect (qatal), imperfect (yiqtol), participle, passive participle, infinitive and imperative. Aramaic narrative uses the perfect and the participle, with the verb 'be', as taught in lessons A4.1.3 and A4.2.2.

Sixth, the stems. The Aramaic Peal, Pael, Haphel and Hophal answer to the Hebrew Qal, Piel, Hiphil and Hophal; the reflexive and passive Hithpeel and Hithpaal answer in part to the Hebrew Niphal and Hithpael. The Aramaic Aphel and Shaphel have no regular Hebrew counterpart in this scheme. The correspondence is rough, and stems are learned with their verbs.

sections.heading: A topic for later: Aramaic in Hebrew books
body: Aramaic does not stand only in its own chapters. Daniel and Ezra are each written partly in Hebrew and partly in Aramaic: the library's Hebrew texts hold the Hebrew chapters of Daniel, and the Aramaic texts hold the rest. Aramaic words also occur inside Hebrew prose in the later books. How they came there, and how to tell them from native Hebrew words, is a question for later study in Hebrew, and this course does not pursue it.

misunderstandings: A Hebrew word with the same letters is not the same Aramaic word. The verbs for 'find' and 'forget', and for 'make' and 'serve', show how far the senses can part.
The consonant correspondences are tendencies. Do not turn a Hebrew word into Aramaic by changing letters: the Aramaic word may not exist, or may be another word altogether.
Aramaic is not Hebrew with the article moved to the end. The determined state also serves as the ordinary noun in many places where Hebrew has no article.
Do not read Aramaic narrative as if it were Hebrew with wayyiqtol forms. Look for the perfect and the participle.

deeper.heading: Why a cognate shifts
body: A word shared by two related languages need not keep its sense in both. In the sister languages the older word was used in different ways, and each language chose different words for the common jobs. The Hebrew choice of one verb for 'find' and the Aramaic choice of another is a matter of the history of each language and not a mistake of either.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in haste, and said thus unto him: 'I have found a man of the children of the captivity of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpretation.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The Haphel perfect, first person singular, of the Aramaic verb 'find': Arioch says 'I have found a man'. The Hebrew verb with the same letters means 'forget', which would make nonsense of the verse. Hebrew would use another verb here.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The king answered and said to the Chaldeans: 'The thing is certain with me; if ye make not known unto me the dream and the interpretation thereof, ye shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The Aramaic noun for 'word' or 'matter', with the ending of the determined state: the king says that the matter is certain with him. Hebrew has a word with the same letters, but the usual Hebrew noun for 'word' and 'thing' is a different one.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Then were these men brought before the king.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The Peal perfect of the verb 'say', here 'commanded': the king in his rage 'said to bring' the three men. The verb is a perfect, which carries the narrative; Hebrew narrative would more often have a wayyiqtol.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Daniel spoke and said: Blessed be the name of God from everlasting even unto everlasting; for wisdom and might are His;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: An imperfect of the verb 'be' with the prefix לְ-, meaning 'let it be': Daniel blesses the name of God. Where Hebrew would use a jussive with the prefix י-, Aramaic puts לְ- on the third person.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The Chaldeans answered before the king, and said: 'There is not a man upon the earth that can declare the king's matter; forasmuch as no great and powerful king hath asked such a thing of any magician, or enchanter, or Chaldean.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The word for 'there is' in the negative clause, and the relative דִּי after it: 'there is not a man upon the earth who can declare the king's matter'. The Hebrew counterparts are the word for 'there is' and the relative אֲשֶׁר.
